candidates.attacker_control: The element name is attacker-supplied HTML (`element.localpart` comes from the untrusted document). The policy is trusted, so the branch becomes reachable only if the deployed policy defines a tag with action="validate" whose name is a suffix of "style" (e.g. "e", "le", "tyle").
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the DOM scanner's equivalent decision (exact `equals` plus `policy.getStyleTag() != null`), confirming intended semantics; enumerated all `<tag name=...>` entries in all six bundled policy XMLs and found no tag named "e", "le", "yle" or "tyle" (only the literal "style" tag, for which endsWith and equals both evaluate true), so the bundled default configurations are not demonstrably exploitable; considered whether the branch could be reached for unknown/encoded tags (tag==null and encode paths are handled by earlier branches, so `isStyle` is only evaluated for policy tags with action validate); no code was executed.
candidates.impact: Sanitizer logic confusion on a security-critical branch: attacker-controlled element content is re-interpreted by the CSS parser/serializer path for a class of element names, potentially allowing content the normal validate path would have escaped/serialized differently (CSS-injection/XSS-style bypass) when such a policy tag exists. Concrete exploitation with the bundled default policies could not be demonstrated from source alone; reachable impact is bounded by which attacker-controlled markup the configured policy maps to a validate action with a suffix-of-"style" name.
candidates.prerequisites: Application scans untrusted HTML through the SAX path (AntiSamy.scan with SAX scan type / AntiSamySAXScanner, including AntiSamy.scan(Reader,Writer,Policy)) and uses a custom policy containing a validate-action tag named a suffix of "style"; none of the six bundled policies (antisamy.xml, -anythinggoes, -ebay, -myspace, -slashdot, -tinymce) define such a tag, so the bundled defaults do not expose it.
candidates.root_cause: MagicSAXFilter.startElement computes `boolean isStyle = "style".endsWith(element.localpart);`. String.endsWith on the literal "style" returns true not only for the actual `<style>` element but for any element name that is a suffix of "style" (e.g. "e", "le", "tyle"). The branch is gated only by `tag.isAction("validate")` and the policy tag lookup, not by an exact name match or `policy.getStyleTag()`. The DOM counterpart uses the safe form `"style".equals(tagNameLowerCase) && policy.getStyleTag() != null` (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:357), showing the intended check.
candidates.title: SAX filter misidentifies style elements via endsWith instead of equality, routing other validate-action tags' content through the CSS path
candidates.trace: startElement(): tag = policy.getTagByLowercaseName(element.localpart.toLowerCase()); if tag.isAction("validate") -> isStyle = "style".endsWith(element.localpart) (line 280) -> when isStyle, push Ops.CSS, set cssAttributes = validattributes, and accumulate all character data (lines 360-363 and 103-106) -> endElement() runs CssScanner.scanStyleSheet over the untrusted text and, if the cleaned result is non-empty, emits the element with the validated attributes plus the CSS-cleaned text (lines 162-203). A non-style element is therefore treated as a style element: its content is interpreted/rewritten as CSS instead of following normal HTML validation/serialization semantics, and its attributes are re-emitted under the CSS branch.
candidates.unverified: End-to-end exploitability was not demonstrated; the finding depends on a custom policy defining a validate-action tag that is a suffix of "style" and on SAX-path usage. Whether this line is an injected regression or longstanding upstream behavior could not be established without an upstream diff (no VCS metadata is present in the snapshot).

coverage_summary: Reviewed all Java sources under src/main/java (scanners, Policy/InternalPolicy, model classes, CSS scanner/handler/validator/parser, serializers, utilities) and all bundled resources (six antisamy policy XMLs, message bundles, pom.xml, CI configs, README/SECURITY). Binary/jar contents and the referenced antisamy.xsd are not present in the snapshot and could not be inspected; no tests are present.
limitations: No VCS metadata or upstream reference copy is available, so injected-regression vs. long-standing upstream behavior cannot be distinguished definitively.
No test suite is included, so reachability/exploitability of the identified logic branch could not be validated; no code was executed (per instructions).
The referenced schema resource 'antisamy.xsd' is absent from the visible file list, so actual runtime schema-validation behavior and whether policy loads succeed could not be verified.
Only the bundled policies were surveyed for exploitable tag names; a custom policy is the stated prerequisite for the candidate and its content is outside the snapshot.
Dependency classes (NekoHTML, Xalan serializer, Batik parser) are not part of the snapshot, so serializer behavior for CDATA/style content and parser hardening settings could not be inspected.

rejected_leads.lead: CssHandler.importStyle discards the return value of URI.normalize() (src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/css/CssHandler.java:307-321), so the 'canonicalize the URI' step is a no-op before offsiteURL/onsiteURL matching.
rejected_leads.reason: Real code smell, but impact is confined to the optional embedStyleSheets=true path and the same URIs are still matched against policy regexes before being fetched; no clear trust-boundary violation demonstrable from source, and it appears to be longstanding upstream code.

rejected_leads.lead: Policy include/entity resolution validates only the base URL: verifyLocalUrl(baseUrl) is called, then `new URL(baseUrl, href)` may resolve an absolute remote href and url.openStream() is invoked (Policy.java:563-594, 1007-1040).
rejected_leads.reason: The href comes from the policy file, a trusted configuration input; an attacker who controls the policy include already controls sanitization. No attacker-controlled path from untrusted HTML into this code was established.

rejected_leads.lead: Dynamic-attribute matching uses prefix startsWith on keys derived with an off-by-one substring (Policy.java:722-734, 955-965), so attributes starting with 'data' (not only 'data-') are allowed with the permissive 'anything' regexp when allowDynamicAttributes=true.
rejected_leads.reason: Broadens an intentionally permissive feature but no source-level path to script execution (event handlers are on* attributes, not data*); concrete security impact not shown.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtil.decode/encode use Matcher.matches() before replaceAll (XMLUtil.java:158-208), so entity decoding is a no-op for mixed strings; and AntiSamyDOMScanner.stripNonValidXMLCharacters uses matches() instead of find() (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:722-729), so invalid XML characters mixed with valid text are not stripped.
rejected_leads.reason: Primarily functional/robustness defects (possible parse-exception/DoS) rather than a demonstrable sanitizer bypass; no attacker-controlled path to script execution established from source.

rejected_leads.lead: Dependency/config exposure: neko-htmlunit 2.24 and batik-css 1.14 are old, and getDomParser() silently continues when the 'enforce-strict-attribute-names' feature is unavailable (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:217-222).
rejected_leads.reason: Dependency/runtime-classpath concerns; the snapshot provides no dependency source to review and no evidence about which parser actually loads at runtime, so this cannot be asserted as a source vulnerability.

summary: AntiSamy 1.6.6-dev snapshot (HTML/CSS sanitizer): reviewed all 54 visible files (Java scanners, Policy/model classes, CSS handler/validator, util classes, serializers, bundled policy XMLs). The strongest source-backed lead is an incorrect tag-identity check in the SAX filter: MagicSAXFilter treats any validate-action element whose name is a suffix of the literal "style" as the CSS-bearing style element (`"style".endsWith(element.localpart)`) instead of an equality check, whereas the DOM scanner uses an exact match plus a policy check. With the bundled policies no tag name is a suffix of "style", so end-to-end exploitation could not be shown from source alone; it is a logic defect on a security-critical branch that becomes reachable with a custom policy defining such a validate tag, changing how untrusted element content is routed (CSS scanner/attributes) versus normal HTML validation. No candidate was runtime-confirmed.
